stem: You need a copy of your contract, a leave form, and confirmation that your health insurance is active. Which office do you go to?
options: 人事室 Personnel Office
學務處 Office of Student Affairs
教務處 Office of Academic Affairs
總務處 Office of General Affairs
why: The 人事室 holds your contract, leave records, insurance enrolment and work-permit paperwork. In a small school this may be one person, sometimes combined with 會計室 / 主計室. Learn their name in your first week — they will handle more of your life in Taiwan than anyone else at the school.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: Your timetable has changed, you need to know which textbook a class is using, and you want to book the English classroom. Which office?
options: 學務處 Office of Student Affairs
教務處 Office of Academic Affairs
輔導室 Counseling Office
人事室 Personnel Office
why: 教務處 owns curriculum, timetables, textbooks, exams and room assignment. The person you will deal with most is the 教學組長 (Curriculum Section Chief).
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: A student is injured during your class, and separately you want to know why the whole school is outside on Wednesday morning. Which office covers both?
options: 教務處 Office of Academic Affairs
總務處 Office of General Affairs
學務處 Office of Student Affairs
會計室 Accounting Office
why: 學務處 covers student safety, health (健康中心 and the school nurse), discipline (生教組), clubs and assemblies. Injuries, fights and anything about student behaviour outside the classroom go here.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: A student in your class has stopped speaking, seems withdrawn, and a Taiwanese colleague mentions 「家裡的狀況」— the situation at home. Which office is the right one to raise this with?
options: 教務處 Office of Academic Affairs
總務處 Office of General Affairs
人事室 Personnel Office
輔導室 Counseling Office
why: 輔導室 handles student counselling, special educational needs and referrals to social services. Raising a concern here is always appropriate and is never overreacting. Note: if you ever suspect abuse or neglect, a legal 24-hour reporting duty applies — that is Module 4 in December.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: The projector in your classroom is broken and you have lost your classroom key. Which office?
options: 總務處 Office of General Affairs
教務處 Office of Academic Affairs
學務處 Office of Student Affairs
輔導室 Counseling Office
why: 總務處 handles buildings, equipment, keys, repairs and purchasing. The 事務組 inside it is your practical contact.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: In a Taiwanese elementary school, which single person usually knows the most about an individual student's academic level, family situation, friendships and health?
options: The Principal 校長
The homeroom teacher 導師
The Director of Academic Affairs 教務主任
The English subject teacher
why: The 導師 stays with the same class for years, eats lunch with them, supervises cleaning time, and is the family's main contact. For almost any student-level question — behaviour, absence, a note from home — the 導師 is your first stop, before any office.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: Which description of school job titles is correct?
options: 主任 = section chief; 組長 = director
主任 and 組長 both mean principal
主任 = director of an office; 組長 = section chief within that office
組長 is used only for administrative clerks
why: The hierarchy runs 校長 (Principal) → 主任 (Director, heads a 處/室) → 組長 (Section Chief, heads a 組 inside it) → 老師 (teacher). Addressing someone as 王主任 or 李組長 shows you understand the structure — but calling any of them 老師 is never wrong or rude.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: Your work permit as a foreign teacher at a public school is tied to a specific employer. A nearby cram school (補習班) offers you six well-paid hours on Saturdays. What is the legal position?
options: Fine, because it is outside your contracted school hours
Fine as long as your principal gives verbal permission
Fine as long as you pay tax on the extra income
Illegal unless a separate permit is obtained for that employer — a fine of NT$30,000–150,000 and possible loss of your right to stay
why: Under the Employment Service Act a foreign national may not work without a permit for that specific work and employer. Article 68 sets a fine of NT$30,000–150,000, and the authorities may revoke the permit and order departure. Your principal cannot authorise this — only the competent authority can. This is the single most common way a foreign teacher loses their position in Taiwan.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: You move to a new apartment in November. What must you do about your ARC (外僑居留證)?
options: Apply to change your registered address at a National Immigration Agency service centre within 30 days
Nothing until the ARC is renewed
Tell your school only — the school will handle it
Nothing; the ARC address is not required to be current
why: Your ARC address must be kept current with the 內政部移民署, within 30 days of the move. An out-of-date address causes real problems later — renewal, tax documents and official mail all go to the registered address. Tell your Personnel Office too, but the legal filing is yours.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: When does your National Health Insurance (健保) coverage as a school employee begin?
options: After six months of residence in Taiwan
From your first day of employment — your employer enrols you
Only after you apply in person at an NHI office
Only after your ARC has been valid for one year
why: As an employed person you are enrolled by the school from your start date, with premiums deducted from salary. You will receive a 健保卡 — carry it; it is what makes a clinic visit cost a few hundred NT dollars instead of several thousand. A spouse and children living in Taiwan can usually be enrolled as dependants; ask Personnel.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: In Taiwanese income tax, what does the 183-day rule determine?
options: How long you may stay in Taiwan on one ARC
When you become eligible for National Health Insurance
Whether you are taxed as a resident at progressive rates, or have the higher non-resident flat rate withheld from your salary
When you may apply for permanent residence
why: 183 days or more within a single calendar year (1 Jan–31 Dec) makes you a tax resident, filing an annual return at progressive rates. Under 183 days in that calendar year, salary is subject to non-resident withholding at a higher flat rate. This matters most in your first and last partial years. The annual filing period is 1–31 May, for the previous calendar year.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: A typhoon is approaching. Who decides whether your school closes tomorrow?
options: Your principal
The Ministry of Education
Each teacher decides individually
The county or city government — for you, the Changhua County Government
why: Closure (停止上班上課) is announced by the local government, usually the evening before or by about 5:00 a.m. Check the Changhua County Government announcement or local news, not just your school's LINE group. If the county announces closure you do not go in, and you are not expected to work from home unless your contract says so.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: You wake up with a fever and cannot teach today. What is the correct first action?
options: Follow the leave procedure in your contract — notify Personnel and your co-teacher before the school day starts, and submit the leave form
Post in the school LINE group and wait to see if someone replies
Message your students' parents directly
Simply do not attend; sick days do not need advance notice
why: Foreign English teachers are employed under a contract, not under the Teachers' Act, so your leave entitlement and procedure come from your contract and your school's rules — not from the regulations governing Taiwanese certified teachers. The number of days, the notice period and the form differ between schools, so confirm the exact procedure with Personnel in Week 1. Notifying early matters: someone has to cover your classes.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: Which hotline should a foreign resident call for 24-hour English-language help with everyday life in Taiwan — visas, health insurance, housing, general questions?
why: 1990 is the Foreigners in Taiwan hotline: free, 24 hours, in English, Japanese, Vietnamese, Indonesian and Thai. Learn the others too — 110 police, 119 fire and ambulance, 113 Protection Hotline for child abuse, domestic violence and sexual assault (English available; you will use this in Module 4), 1957 social welfare.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: You see a sign on an office door reading 學務處. What is inside?
options: Academic Affairs
General Affairs
Student Affairs
Personnel
why: 學 = study/student, 務 = affairs, 處 = office. Its neighbour 教務處 (教 = teaching) is Academic Affairs. Reading these five signs is the fastest way to stop needing a guide around your own school.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: The school calendar (行事曆) tells you all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Exam weeks
Sports day and the school anniversary
Make-up school days that fall on Saturdays
Which textbook each grade is using
why: The 行事曆 is the single most useful document you will receive all year. Ask 教務處 for a copy in Week 1 and put every date in your phone — especially the make-up school days (補課日), which are working Saturdays that compensate for extended holidays. Textbooks come from 教務處 separately.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: 朝會 refers to:
options: A whole-school morning assembly, often outdoors, with announcements and sometimes a flag-raising ceremony
A staff meeting held after school
A parent-teacher conference
The morning cleaning period
why: 朝 = morning, 會 = gathering. Ask your co-teacher which mornings it runs and whether foreign teachers are expected to attend and stand with a class — practice varies between schools, and simply showing up the first time is the easiest way to find out.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: After lunch in most Taiwanese elementary and junior high schools, the lights go off and students rest at their desks. This is:
options: An optional break students may skip
午休 — a scheduled quiet/nap period, part of the school day
Unsupervised free time
A period reserved for make-up lessons
why: 午休 is normally 20–40 minutes, supervised by the homeroom teacher, and is treated as part of the school day. Do not schedule activities, meetings or noisy preparation during it, and do not read a sleeping class as a discipline problem.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: 打掃時間 (cleaning time) means:
options: Cleaning staff clean the school while students are in class
A punishment assigned to misbehaving students
Students clean their own classrooms and assigned areas of the school as part of the daily timetable
An optional after-school volunteer activity
why: Students cleaning the school is standard practice and is treated as part of their education — not as labour and not as punishment. If your class has an assigned area you may be asked to supervise. Joining in occasionally, even briefly, is noticed and appreciated far out of proportion to the effort.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: A well-known cram school offers you Saturday work. The owner says: “Many foreign teachers here do this. Your school will never know, and we have never had a problem.” Your best response is:
options: Accept — the risk appears to be low in practice
Accept, but ask your principal for verbal permission first
Accept, and declare the income in May to make it legitimate
Decline, unless a separate work permit is obtained for that employer — the exposure is a fine and loss of your right to stay, and it is enforced
why: “Everyone does it” and “nobody checks” are not defences. Declaring the income does not cure the permit problem — the offence is working without authorisation for that employer, not failing to pay tax. Your principal has no power to waive it. Enforcement is usually triggered by something unrelated: a labour inspection, a dispute with the cram school, or an ARC renewal.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: A parent finds you on LINE and adds you directly, then asks detailed questions about their child's progress — and about another student in the class. The most appropriate response is:
options: Reply politely, decline to discuss any other student, redirect substantive matters to the homeroom teacher, and tell your co-teacher the contact happened
Block the parent without explanation
Answer fully; good parent communication is part of the job
Ignore the messages entirely
why: Two separate issues. Discussing a different student's behaviour or performance with a parent is a privacy problem — that is Module 7 in April. And in Taiwanese schools the 導師 is the designated channel to families; going around them creates confusion and undercuts them. Keeping your co-teacher informed protects you both: never let them hear about a parent contact from the parent.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: It is March. You are fairly sure you want to return next year, but nobody has said anything about renewal. What should you do?
options: Wait — the school will raise it when they are ready
Raise it yourself with Personnel and the principal, because staffing plans and budget cycles are decided months before the school year ends
Assume renewal is automatic unless told otherwise
Wait until June, closer to the contract expiry
why: Schools plan headcount, funding applications and recruitment well before the year ends. Silence is not a signal about your performance — it usually means nobody thought to tell the foreign teacher about a process conducted in Chinese. Asking early is not pushy; it is what a returning colleague is expected to do. Ask specifically about the timeline, the paperwork, and whether your work permit and ARC renew in step with the contract.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: At 8:10 a.m. your co-teacher asks you to cover her 8:40 class — she has been called into a meeting. You have never taught that class and have no materials. The best response is:
options: Refuse; covering another teacher's class is outside your contract
Agree, and use the time for unplanned free talk
Agree if you reasonably can, ask what the class is working on and whether the homeroom teacher will be there — and raise the pattern with her later if it becomes frequent
Agree, then report the request to Personnel
why: Short-notice cover is normal and reciprocal in Taiwanese schools, and saying yes builds real goodwill. But “yes now” and “let's talk about this” later is a legitimate combination. Raise the pattern directly and privately with your co-teacher first — going to an office before speaking to the person concerned makes her lose face and will damage the working relationship far more than the original request did.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: You are leaving Taiwan at the end of June and will not return. Which of these is most likely to be forgotten and to cause a real problem?
options: Returning your classroom keys
Saying goodbye to your classes
Handing over your teaching materials
Settling your tax before departure, and closing out NHI, pension and ARC obligations in the right order
why: A departing resident generally must settle income tax for the current year before leaving rather than waiting for the following May, and there are separate steps for NHI withdrawal, any pension or severance entitlement under your contract, closing a bank account, and surrendering or letting the ARC lapse. Start this with Personnel six weeks before departure, not in the final week. Doing it badly can cause problems if you ever apply to work in Taiwan again.
mz: 校園組織與你的法律身分

stem: Roughly when does the first semester (上學期) of a Taiwanese school year run?
options: Late August or early September to mid or late January
September to December
October to March
January to June
why: The first semester runs from late August or early September to mid or late January, and the second (下學期) from mid February to the end of June. Winter vacation sits between them, timed around Lunar New Year — which is why its dates move from year to year.

stem: What is 段考?
options: A staff meeting held each month
A periodic exam — each semester usually has two or three, plus a final
A parent-teacher conference
The daily cleaning period
why: 段考 are the periodic exams that structure each semester. During an exam period the timetable is rewritten, and your English lesson may be shortened, moved, merged or cancelled — sometimes at a day's notice.

stem: You notice a Saturday marked on the school calendar as a school day. What does that mean?
options: An optional enrichment day for students who want it
A day for teachers only, with no students
A make-up school day (補課日) — a full working day you are expected to attend
A typographical error worth ignoring
why: When a national holiday falls next to a weekend, Taiwan often bridges the gap and makes the day up on a Saturday. That Saturday is a normal school day: full timetable, full attendance, you included. The dates are published far in advance — which is why missing one is the least forgivable first-year mistake.

stem: Which document is the authoritative source for school dates?
options: The school LINE group
Your contract
The Ministry of Education website
The school calendar 行事曆
why: The 行事曆 is the source of truth; the LINE group is where same-day changes get announced, usually in Chinese; your co-teacher is who you ask when you cannot decode either. Get the calendar from 教務處 and put all of it in your phone.

stem: You have designed a six-week project that builds week on week. Where should it NOT start?
options: Four weeks before an exam period, so that it runs into 段考
Immediately after a long holiday
At the beginning of a semester
In the second half of the second semester
why: Anything that depends on continuity will break in an exam week — lessons get shortened, moved or cancelled. Ask 教務處 for the exam dates at the start of each semester and plan your units between them, not through them.

stem: Sports day (運動會) is coming. What should you expect?
options: It affects only PE lessons
It is often held on a Saturday, and weeks of rehearsal beforehand also take lesson time
It is optional for teachers who do not coach
It replaces a single afternoon
why: Sports day is a whole-school event, frequently on a Saturday, and the rehearsals in the weeks before it also eat into normal lessons. Attendance is expected and being visible matters — this is one of the days colleagues remember whether you showed up.

stem: Your class has a 校外教學 next Tuesday, the day you normally teach them. What happens to your lesson?
options: It is rescheduled automatically to another slot
You teach the students who did not go
It simply does not happen that week
You are required to join the trip
why: A field trip is a full-day class outing and your lesson with that class does not happen. You may or may not be invited along — ask, rather than assuming either way. Plan for the loss instead of trying to recover the lesson.

stem: You are told there is a 教學觀摩 and colleagues will watch one of your lessons. This is:
options: A disciplinary inspection prompted by a complaint
Something you may decline without consequence
A test that affects your contract renewal
A routine professional activity — colleagues observe and discuss afterwards
why: Observed lessons are ordinary professional practice in Taiwanese schools, and being asked is not a signal that something is wrong. Ask in advance what the focus is and who will be present; treating it as normal is both accurate and the fastest way to be treated as a colleague.

stem: Whether you work during winter and summer vacation is determined by:
options: Your contract
National holiday rules
Ministry of Education regulations
The homeroom teachers' rota
why: Your contract decides it, and schools differ. Common arrangements include a 返校日 (return-to-school day), a winter or summer camp, or planning and preparation duties. Read the clause before you make travel plans, and confirm with 人事室 rather than with a colleague's recollection.

stem: You want to take leave to fly home in April. When should you raise it?
options: A week before, so plans are still flexible
As early as you can, and before booking any flight
Only after buying the ticket, so the dates are fixed
Leave is your entitlement; no notice is needed
why: Ask early, and never book flights before the leave is confirmed. Someone has to cover your classes, and requests around Lunar New Year, exam weeks and the end of term are the hardest to grant. The order matters: approval first, ticket second.

stem: At 8:05 a.m. your co-teacher tells you today's lesson is cancelled for a rehearsal nobody mentioned. The most useful response is:
options: Point out that you were not consulted and that this is unprofessional
Ask 教務處 to reinstate the lesson
Accept it, use the time for preparation, and start asking her weekly what is changing next week
Teach the lesson anyway in a different room
why: Late notice about whole-school events is normal here and is rarely aimed at you — the information existed in Chinese somewhere upstream and did not get translated. The fix is systemic, not confrontational: ask your co-teacher once a week whether anything is changing. Ninety seconds removes most of what feels like being kept in the dark.

stem: A parent meeting (親師座談會) is scheduled. What should you do?
options: Assume you are not involved unless told otherwise
Ask parents to contact you directly afterwards
Prepare a full progress report on every student
Ask in advance whether you are expected to appear or introduce yourself
why: Practice varies: some schools want the foreign teacher to appear briefly and say hello, others do not involve you at all. Ask in advance rather than either turning up unexpectedly or being absent when you were expected. Individual student discussions belong to the homeroom teacher.

stem: Who announces that schools are closed for a typhoon?
options: The county or city government — for you, Changhua County
Your principal
The Ministry of Education
The Central Weather Administration
why: The local government announces closure, usually the evening before or by about 5:00 a.m. Check the county announcement or local news rather than relying on the school LINE group alone. If the county closes schools, you do not go in.

stem: Which is the best weekly habit for staying ahead of schedule changes?
options: Checking the Ministry of Education website
Asking your co-teacher whether anything is changing next week
Reading the school LINE group carefully every evening
Asking students what is happening
why: The calendar covers what was planned months ago; the LINE group covers today, usually in Chinese. The weekly question to your co-teacher covers the gap between them — which is precisely where a foreign teacher usually gets caught out.

stem: 下學期 means:
options: After-school programme
The lower grades
The second semester
Evening classes
why: 上 = upper/first, 下 = lower/second, 學期 = semester. So 上學期 is the first semester and 下學期 the second, running from mid February to the end of June.

stem: 校慶 refers to:
options: A school inspection
A staff training day
A graduation ceremony
The school's anniversary celebration
why: 校 = school, 慶 = celebration. The school's birthday, sometimes combined with sports day: performances, alumni, local dignitaries, and no normal lessons.

stem: 返校日 means:
options: A day students return to school during a vacation
The first day of the school year
A day for parents to visit
A make-up class on a Saturday
why: 返 = return, 校 = school. A day during winter or summer vacation when students — and often staff — come in. Whether you are required to attend depends on your contract.

stem: Where do you get a copy of the school calendar?
options: 人事室 Personnel Office
教務處 Office of Academic Affairs
總務處 Office of General Affairs
輔導室 Counseling Office
why: 教務處 owns the calendar along with timetables, textbooks and exams. Ask in your first week of each semester — do not wait for it to be handed to you.

stem: Your English lesson is cancelled during an exam period. This means:
options: Your subject is not valued at this school
Something has gone wrong and you should ask why
This is the normal rhythm of an exam week
You should teach the lesson to a different class instead
why: Exam periods rewrite the timetable for everyone, and it is not a comment on English or on you. The useful response is planning: get the exam dates early and build your units around them rather than into them.

stem: You have planned a six-week unit. Looking at the calendar, an exam period, sports day rehearsals and a field trip will remove four of your six lessons with that class. What is the best response?
options: Teach the unit anyway and compress it into the sessions that survive
Move the unit to the second semester and teach revision until then
Ask 教務處 to protect your lesson slots
Redesign it as self-contained lessons that work in any order, and save the continuous unit for a clear stretch
why: Compressing a continuous unit into fragments teaches it badly, and asking for protected slots against a whole-school event will not succeed and will cost you goodwill. Building a bank of standalone lessons for broken weeks — and saving continuous units for the clear stretches — is what experienced teachers here actually do. Read the calendar first, then design.

stem: For the third time this month a lesson has been cancelled at short notice, and you only found out from a student. What is the most effective thing to do?
options: Ask your co-teacher for a standing weekly check-in on next week's changes, and ask to be added to whichever LINE group carries the announcements
Raise it with the principal as a professional-respect issue
Email 教務處 asking to be notified in writing of every change
Accept it as unchangeable and stop planning in advance
why: This is almost never about respect — the information existed in Chinese in a channel you are not in. Fixing the channel fixes the problem; escalating it as a grievance does not, and makes the person who could actually help you defensive. Ask for the standing check-in and the group access, and the same problem stops recurring.

stem: You want two weeks of leave over Lunar New Year to travel. When and how should you handle it?
options: Book flights now while they are cheap, then request the leave
Raise it with 人事室 months ahead, confirm in writing what your contract allows during 寒假, and book only after approval
Ask a colleague what other foreign teachers have done and follow that
Wait until January, when the schedule is settled
why: Lunar New Year is the hardest period to get approved, and whether you are even required to work during 寒假 is a contract question that varies by school. Get the answer in writing from 人事室 well ahead, then book. Colleagues' recollections of what someone else did are not a reliable guide to your own contract.

stem: You are asked to help at sports day, which falls on a Saturday. Before agreeing, the sensible thing to establish is:
options: Nothing — attending school events is simply part of the job
Whether you will be paid overtime, raised firmly at the time of the request
Whether your contract treats it as a working day, and whether compensatory time off applies — asked early and in a low-key way with 人事室
Whether other foreign teachers are attending
why: Being present at whole-school events genuinely matters to how you are seen, so start from yes. But whether a working Saturday is already counted in your hours, and whether time off in lieu applies, is a real contract question worth settling once — quietly, with 人事室, well before the day. Asked early it is administration; raised on the morning itself it reads as reluctance.

stem: A make-up school day (補課日) falls on a Saturday you had already committed to something personal. What is the right move?
options: Skip it — Saturdays are not really school days
Tell your co-teacher on the Friday so somebody knows
Swap with another teacher informally
Treat it as a normal working day requiring leave: request leave as early as you can, through the normal procedure
why: A 補課日 is a full working school day in every respect, so missing it needs approved leave like any other absence. The dates are published in advance precisely so this clash can be spotted early — check the whole calendar against your own commitments at the start of each semester, not the week before.

stem: Zero corporal punishment in Taiwanese schools is established by:
options: Statute — Article 8 of the Educational Fundamental Act
Ministry of Education advice that schools may adopt
Individual school policy, which varies between schools
A collective agreement between teachers' associations
why: Article 8 of the Educational Fundamental Act (教育基本法) protects students' right to bodily autonomy and to the development of their personality, and requires that they suffer no corporal punishment or bullying. Taiwan banned corporal punishment in schools in 2006. This is law, not local preference — no principal can authorise an exception.

stem: A class is noisy, so you make them do twenty press-ups. This is:
options: Acceptable — it is exercise, not punishment
Capable of being corporal punishment, because requiring physical exertion or positions as a penalty is covered
Acceptable if you join in
Acceptable for older students only
why: The definition covers requiring a student to hold or perform particular physical actions for the purpose of punishment, where the student objectively suffers physical pain or harm. Press-ups, laps, squats, kneeling and holding arms out all fall in scope. “It's just exercise” is the most common misunderstanding in this module, and intent to be harsh is not required.

stem: Standing reflection (站立反省) is permitted, but with what limits?
options: No limits, provided the student can see the board
No more than ten minutes, once per week
No more than one class period at a time, and no more than two hours cumulatively in a day
It is not permitted at all
why: The Ministry's guidance permits standing reflection expressly, capped at one class period per instance and two hours in total per day. Beyond those limits it stops being a permitted measure and becomes corporal punishment. Knowing the cap is what makes the measure safely usable.

stem: Which of these is on the list of permitted general disciplinary measures?
options: Keeping the whole class in because one student misbehaved
Lowering a student's grade for talking
Making a student kneel at the front
Requiring a written self-reflection
why: A verbal apology or written self-reflection is expressly permitted. The others are not: collective punishment is not on the list, kneeling is a physical position imposed as a penalty, and behaviour must not be punished through academic marks. A reliable working rule — if it is not on the list, do not reach for it.

stem: You want a student to stay after school to finish work. What is required?
options: The guardian's consent
The homeroom teacher's agreement only
Nothing; it is within your normal authority
A written request to 教務處
why: After-school detention requires the guardian's consent. Practically this means it is arranged through the homeroom teacher, who has the family contact — never keep a student back on your own initiative. A child who misses their ride or their after-school class creates a problem far larger than the one you were solving.

stem: A student scores badly on a test. May you impose a punishment for the result?
options: Yes, if the student clearly did not prepare
No — academic results are not a behaviour matter
Yes, if the parents have agreed to it
Only for repeated poor results
why: Punishing a student because of academic performance is outside the purpose of the guidance, which is about behaviour and guidance rather than results. Poor performance is a teaching problem and sometimes a welfare signal — if you are worried, that concern belongs with the homeroom teacher or 輔導室.

stem: A student is using a phone in your lesson. What may you do?
options: Keep it until the end of the week so the lesson is learned
Hand it to another student for safekeeping
Hold it for the remainder of the lesson and return it; anything longer goes through 學務處
Delete anything inappropriate on it before returning it
why: You may temporarily hold an item that is disrupting the lesson, but it must be returned, and anything beyond the end of the lesson should go through 學務處. Never keep a phone overnight, never hand it to another student, and never look through its contents — that last one is a privacy problem of an entirely different order.

stem: Two students start fighting. What is your role?
options: Physically separate them yourself immediately
Send the whole class out and deal with it alone
Wait outside the room until it stops
Protect the other students, call for help at once, and remove a student from the scene only if there is a risk to someone's life or body
why: Where there is a risk of harm to another person's life or body, a student may be removed from the scene and outside help sought. But your first job is the other thirty students and raising the alarm — not becoming the adult who wrestles a teenager, which is how a discipline incident becomes an incident about you. Send a student to the office if you have no other way to call for help.

stem: You ask 學務處 for urgent help with a situation you cannot contain. Under the February 2024 amendment:
options: They cannot refuse a teacher's request for assistance in an urgent situation
They may decline if they are short-staffed
They must first obtain the principal's approval
The request must be made in writing
why: The 2024 amendment made explicit that Student Affairs and Counseling cannot refuse a teacher's request for help when the situation is urgent. Worth knowing: it means asking for help is a right you are exercising, not a favour you are requesting — and not a signal that you cannot manage your class.

stem: A student will not move seats when asked. You take hold of their arm to move them. This is:
options: Fine, since no harm was intended
Not permitted — physical force is prohibited outside the genuine safety exception
Fine, because seating changes are a permitted measure
Fine if the student is small
why: Adjusting seating is a permitted measure; applying physical force to achieve it is not. The exception is a real risk to someone's life or body, which a refusal to move seats is not. When a student will not comply, the answer is your co-teacher or the homeroom teacher — not your hands.

stem: Which of these is the clearest breach of the principle of respecting student dignity?
options: Moving a student to the front of the room
Asking a student to write a reflection
Mocking a student's ability in front of the class
Telling the homeroom teacher about repeated lateness
why: Respect for the student's dignity is a stated principle of the guidance. Public mockery, remarks about a student's intelligence, and comments about their family are not discipline — and unlike a physical breach, this one tends to be witnessed by thirty people who will describe it accurately later.

stem: Where does a foreign English teacher's real influence over classroom behaviour mainly come from?
options: Formal disciplinary authority within the school system
The threat of contacting parents directly
The ability to report students to 學務處
The relationship with the class, lesson design, seating, and a co-teacher who can intervene in Chinese
why: You generally hold no formal disciplinary authority, and that matters far less than it sounds. Design, seating, relationship and a co-teacher who can say in three seconds of Chinese what takes you five minutes of English will settle more classes than any sanction available to you.

stem: What is the correct escalation order for a persistent behaviour problem?
options: Handle it yourself → co-teacher → homeroom teacher (導師) → 學務處
Straight to 學務處, so it is documented from the start
Contact the parents yourself, then the homeroom teacher
Wait until it resolves itself
why: Going straight to the office for small things spends credibility you will want for something serious; never escalating at all is how a class becomes unteachable by March. The 導師 is the pivotal step — they hold the relationship with the student and the family that you do not.

stem: You lose your temper and shout at a class in a way you immediately regret. What is the best next step?
options: Say nothing and hope it is not mentioned
Tell your co-teacher the same day, in your own words
Apologise to the class the following week
Explain yourself to the principal in writing
why: A teacher who reports their own bad moment is a colleague having a bad day. The identical event, first described by a student to a parent three days later, is something else entirely — and by then you are responding rather than explaining. Same day, own words, to the person who works alongside you.

stem: Corporal punishment in the Taiwanese definition means:
options: Hitting a student, and nothing else
Any punishment a student dislikes
Applying physical force, or requiring physical positions or exertion, as a punishment causing pain or harm
Only punishment that leaves a visible mark
why: The definition is functional and broader than hitting: force applied by the teacher, force the teacher has the student or a third party apply, or being made to hold or perform physical actions, for the purpose of punishment, causing objective pain or bodily or mental harm. The second clause is the one that catches teachers who never intended anything of the kind.

stem: Which of these may you do on your own initiative in an English lesson?
options: Contact the student's parents directly
Keep a student after school
Send a student home
Change a student's seat
why: Seating changes are yours to make and are one of the most effective tools you have. Detention needs the guardian's consent, sending a student home is not yours to decide, and family contact goes through the homeroom teacher rather than direct from you.

stem: Who is usually the most effective person to involve when one student's behaviour keeps disrupting your lesson?
options: The homeroom teacher 導師
The principal
The Personnel Office
Another student's parent
why: The 導師 stays with that class for years, knows the student's home situation, and is the family's contact. They can often change in one conversation what you cannot change in a term — and they would rather hear it from you early than discover it late.

stem: Your class is loud, so you keep everyone in during their break. This is:
options: A standard and permitted measure
Not on the list of permitted measures — collective punishment for one student's behaviour is not an accepted approach
Permitted if the whole class was in fact noisy
Permitted once per semester
why: Collective punishment does not appear among the permitted general measures, and the working rule holds: if it is not on the list, do not reach for it. It also reliably damages your relationship with the students who behaved, who are the ones you most need on your side.

stem: You are struggling to manage a class and feel you should handle it alone to avoid looking incompetent. Which is true?
options: Asking for help will be noted as a weakness
You should only ask after a term of trying
In urgent situations 學務處 and 輔導室 cannot refuse a request for help — asking is normal practice, not an admission
Foreign teachers are expected to manage without support
why: The 2024 amendment makes explicit that help cannot be refused in urgent situations, which tells you how the system regards asking. Colleagues here ask each other constantly; the teacher who visibly struggles alone for a term is the one who worries people.

stem: During a co-taught lesson, your co-teacher raps a student's knuckles with a ruler. What is the right response?
options: Say nothing; discipline in her lesson is her business
Challenge her about it immediately, in front of the class
Ask other students afterwards whether this happens often
Say nothing in the room, then raise it with 學務處 or the principal the same day — and if the child appears hurt, the Module 4 duty also applies
why: Confronting a colleague in front of students helps nobody and makes the situation about the two of you. But this is not something you can leave alone either: schools have a formal process for investigating suspected improper discipline, and it starts with someone telling them. Do not canvass students — that contaminates any investigation. If the child appears to have been hurt, the reporting duty from Module 4 runs in parallel and on its own 24-hour clock.

stem: You raise a difficult class with the homeroom teacher, who says: “You just need to be stricter.” What is the most productive response?
options: Ask her to sit in on one lesson and tell you what she sees, and ask which specific students to focus on
Accept it and impose harsher sanctions
Escalate to 學務處 over her head
Conclude that no support is available and manage alone
why: “Be stricter” is usually shorthand for “I don't have a specific picture of what is happening in your room.” Asking her to observe converts vague advice into concrete information and quietly makes her a stakeholder in the outcome. It also puts a Chinese-speaking adult with authority in the room, which frequently changes the class by itself.

stem: A parent complains that you humiliated their child in front of the class. You believe you simply corrected the student. What should you do first?
options: Respond to the parent directly with your account
Write down what happened while you remember it, and tell your co-teacher and the homeroom teacher today
Ask the class to confirm your version
Wait to see whether the school raises it
why: Get your account written and into the school's hands the same day, before the version travelling through the parent network becomes the only one on record. Do not reply to the parent yourself — that is the school's channel — and never ask students to back you up, which turns a manageable complaint into something that looks like pressuring witnesses.

stem: You are asked to supervise a punishment — a group of students running laps for misbehaviour. You think it may be corporal punishment. What do you do?
options: Supervise it, since a Taiwanese colleague decided it
Refuse loudly in front of the students
Do not supervise it; say privately that you understand physical exertion as a penalty to be covered by the prohibition, and ask 學務處 to confirm
Supervise it but report it afterwards
why: Supervising it makes you a participant, and “someone senior told me to” will not help afterwards. Refusing in front of students costs your colleague face for no benefit. Decline quietly, put it as a question about the rule rather than an accusation about them, and let 學務處 give the answer — asking for confirmation is a normal thing a careful teacher does.

stem: A student blocks the doorway and refuses to let you leave the room at the end of a lesson. What is the correct response?
options: Physically move the student aside — you are entitled to leave
Threaten to call the police
Wait silently until the student gives up
Stay calm, do not touch the student, call or send for help, and let a colleague resolve it
why: Nothing here meets the genuine safety exception, so laying hands on the student converts a manageable moment into an incident about you — with witnesses. Stay calm, keep distance, get another adult. In urgent situations 學務處 and 輔導室 cannot refuse a request for help, and this is exactly what that provision is for.

stem: You have a genuine suspicion that a child in your class is being harmed at home. What is the deadline for reporting it?
options: Immediately, and in any case no later than 24 hours
As soon as you have collected enough evidence
Within one school week
At the next staff meeting
why: Both the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act (Art. 53) and the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Art. 50) use the same wording: immediately, and no later than 24 hours. There is no version of this rule that lets you wait and see.

src.label: Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act, Art. 53 →

stem: What standard must be met before you are required to report?
options: You must be certain the abuse happened
You must have a reasonable suspicion
You must have physical evidence
The child must ask you to report it
why: The threshold is suspicion, not certainty. Weighing evidence is the job of social services and the school's designated staff — and quietly deciding for yourself that it is “probably nothing” is the single most common reason a report never gets made.

stem: When does the 24-hour clock start?
options: When you personally decide the case is serious
When the report reaches the county government
When the first member of staff becomes aware — everyone who knows shares the same 24 hours
When the school principal is informed
why: The clock runs from the first staff member's knowledge, and it is shared by everyone who knows. Passing the information to a colleague does not reset it. That is why “I told my co-teacher and assumed she'd handle it” is not a safe answer.

stem: A student shows you bruises. What is your role?
options: Investigate carefully so your report is accurate
Ask the child detailed questions to establish what happened
Photograph the injuries as evidence
Tell the designated person; you are not the investigator
why: You report; you do not investigate. Your own inquiries can contaminate a professional investigation and can make a child's later account less usable. Photographing a child's body is not yours to do and creates its own problems.

stem: A child begins telling you something upsetting and says: “Promise you won't tell anyone.” The right response is:
options: Say honestly that you must tell one person whose job it is to help, and tell the child who that is
Say nothing and let the child keep talking
Promise, so the child feels safe enough to continue
Stop the conversation immediately and walk away
why: A promise you cannot keep is a betrayal the child will feel later, and it damages their trust in every adult after you. Being honest in the moment — “I have to tell one person, and I'll tell you who” — keeps you truthful without shutting the child down. Then stay, and listen without questioning.

stem: Before reporting a suspected case of abuse at home, should you contact the child's parents to check?
options: Yes — parents deserve to hear it from the school first
No — never contact the family first
Yes, but only through the homeroom teacher
Only if the child agrees
why: Never. In a significant share of cases the person you would be warning is the person causing the harm, and warning them puts the child at greater risk and destroys any chance of a clean investigation. Family contact is a decision for social services and the school's designated staff, not for you.

stem: You raise a concern with your co-teacher. She says: “Let's wait — I'll talk to the homeroom teacher tomorrow and we'll decide then.” What should you do?
options: Accept her judgement; she knows the family and the system better
Wait 24 hours and then follow up
Make sure the report is made today — go to the designated person yourself if needed
Let it go; raising it once discharges your duty
why: The duty is personal and the clock is already running. Your co-teacher's seniority does not transfer your obligation to her, and “we'll decide tomorrow” is exactly how a 24-hour deadline gets missed. Do it without drama: tell her you are going to pass it on today because of the time limit. That framing is factual, not an accusation.

stem: Which of these makes a mandatory report unnecessary?
options: The child says they fell down the stairs
The family is known to the school and considered respectable
Another teacher says the child exaggerates
None of these
why: None of them. Children very often explain injuries in ways that protect the adult harming them, reputations tell you nothing, and second-hand character assessments are not evidence. Every one of these is a familiar reason a report was not filed — which is precisely why the legal threshold is suspicion and the decision is not left to you.

stem: Under Article 53, what protection does the person making the report have?
options: The reporter's identity is kept confidential by law
None — the report is public record
Protection only if the report turns out to be correct
Protection only for Taiwanese nationals
why: Article 53 makes the reporter's identity confidential by law. And a report made in good faith that turns out to be mistaken is not a problem — that outcome is designed into the system. A report never made is the failure the law is aimed at.

stem: An educator who fails to report without justification faces:
options: A verbal warning only
An administrative fine
Immediate deportation
Nothing; the duty is advisory
why: Failure to report without legitimate cause carries a fine of NT$6,000–60,000 under Art. 100 of the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act, and NT$6,000–30,000 under Art. 62 of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act. The penalty is not the real reason to report — but it does tell you how seriously the system treats this.

stem: It is a Saturday. You have a serious concern and cannot reach anyone at your school. What do you do?
options: Wait until Monday morning
Post in the school LINE group
Call 113, the Protection Hotline — 24 hours, English available
Contact the parents yourself
why: 113 operates 24 hours with English available, and you can also file online through 關懷e起來 (ecare.mohw.gov.tw) at any time. If a child is in immediate physical danger, call 110 first. “The office was closed” is not a justification for missing the deadline.

stem: Who is allowed to make a child-protection report?
options: Only mandated professionals such as teachers, doctors and police
Only the school, acting as an institution
Only a Taiwanese citizen
Anyone at all — the law expressly permits any person to report
why: Article 53 requires certain professionals to report and separately permits anyone to report. That second paragraph matters to you: if you have told the school and you are not confident anything happened, you can still make the report yourself. Nobody's permission is needed.

stem: After a child discloses something to you, what should you write down?
options: The date, time, place, and the child's words as closely as you can recall them
Your assessment of whether the child is telling the truth
Nothing — written notes can be used against you
A summary in your own words, interpreting what they meant
why: Record facts, not conclusions: when, where, who was present, and what the child actually said — their words, not your paraphrase. Do it as soon as you are alone, while it is fresh. Your interpretation is not useful to an investigation and can actively distort it.

stem: A student tells you they have been cutting themselves and asks you not to tell anyone. What do you do?
options: Keep the confidence to preserve their trust
Tell 輔導室 immediately and do not leave the student alone
Wait and watch for a few days
Tell the class homeroom teacher at the end of term
why: Do not leave them alone, do not promise secrecy, and get 輔導室 (Counseling) involved immediately — walk them there yourself if you can. This is also reportable through the campus safety system. The 24-hour framing applies, but the practical answer is “now”, not “today”.

stem: Which number is Taiwan's 24-hour Protection Hotline for child abuse, domestic violence and sexual assault?
why: 113. English is available. Save it now, alongside 110 (police), 119 (fire and ambulance) and 1990 (Foreigners in Taiwan hotline).

stem: For educators in Taiwan, reporting suspected child abuse is:
options: A professional courtesy
A school policy that varies between schools
Optional for teachers who are not Taiwanese nationals
A legal duty set out in statute
why: It is a statutory duty. Article 53 of the Child and Juvenile Welfare and Rights Protection Act names educators specifically, and Article 50 of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act does the same. Your school will treat you as carrying this duty — and the right action is the same either way.

stem: What you saw does not fit neatly into any of the listed categories of harm. What does that mean?
options: The law includes a general “any other harm” category — report it
You should wait until it fits a category
No report is required
You should ask the child which category applies
why: Article 53 ends with a deliberate catch-all covering any other circumstance of harm. It exists precisely so that “it didn't quite fit the list” can never be the reason a child went unreported. If you are worried, that is enough to pass it on.

stem: A child starts telling you something serious. Which response is best in the moment?
options: Ask detailed follow-up questions so you have the full picture
Listen without questioning, thank them, and tell them what happens next
Bring another teacher over immediately so the child can repeat it
Suggest they write it down instead
why: Listen; do not interview. Repeated questioning — and being made to repeat a disclosure to a second adult — is harmful to the child and weakens the account for the people who will investigate properly. Your job in the room is to stay calm, listen, and be honest about the next step.

stem: Who at your school should receive your report first?
options: The principal, always
Whichever colleague you know best
The designated person named in your school's prevention rules — usually 學務處 or 輔導室
The county Education Department
why: Every school names designated staff in its own prevention rules; in most schools that is 學務處 (Student Affairs) or 輔導室 (Counseling). They file both the campus-safety report and the social-services report. Find out the name and extension at your school before you ever need it.

stem: You report a concern to your co-teacher, who is senior to you and knows the family. She says: “I know this family. It's not what you think. Leave it with me.” Two days later nothing appears to have happened. What is the correct action?
options: Trust her judgement — she has the context you lack
Raise it again with her and give her another week
Take it straight to the county Education Department
Report it yourself now, to the designated person or via 113 / 關懷e起來, and tell her you have done so
why: The duty is personal and the deadline has already passed. Anyone may file a report, so nothing is blocking you. Telling her you have done it — plainly, without accusation — is better than doing it behind her back: it keeps the working relationship survivable and makes clear you acted on a legal obligation rather than on distrust of her.

stem: You made a report six weeks ago. Nobody has told you anything since, and the child seems unchanged. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing — confidentiality means you are usually not told the outcome, and no news is not evidence of no action
The report was probably dismissed as unfounded
You should re-report the identical concern weekly
You should ask the child directly what happened
why: You are generally not entitled to case information, and silence tells you nothing about what is happening. What you should do is keep reporting anything new — each fresh concern is its own report — and keep your own dated notes. Asking the child what social services did is not appropriate.

stem: A parent confronts you angrily, having worked out that a report about their family came from your class. The best response is:
options: Deny that you made any report

Say that you are legally required to pass on any concern about a child, that you cannot discuss an individual case, and refer them to the school — then tell your principal about the confrontation the same day
Explain your reasoning and the evidence you had
Apologise and say you will not do it again
why: Do not litigate the case at the school gate and do not disclose details. State the duty in general terms, decline to discuss specifics, and disengage. Then inform your principal and Personnel the same day — an angry parent contact should reach school leadership from you first, not from the parent. Your identity as reporter is protected by law, and your school should be protecting you here.

stem: You are genuinely unsure whether what you noticed is serious enough to report. Which reasoning is correct?
options: Uncertainty means you should observe for another week before deciding
You should consult two colleagues and follow the majority view
Uncertainty is exactly the situation the low threshold is designed for — report it
You should report only if you would be willing to testify
why: The threshold is suspicion precisely so that uncertain cases still reach the people trained to assess them. “I'll watch for another week” is the single most common failure mode, and it is the one the deadline exists to prevent. A good-faith report that turns out to be wrong costs nothing; the reverse error costs a child.

stem: During a lesson, a student mentions something that suggests a member of school staff — not a family member — may be harming a child. What changes?
options: You should wait and gather corroboration from other students
You should raise it privately with that colleague first
You should say nothing without proof, because an accusation could end a career
Nothing changes; report it exactly as you would any other concern
why: The duty is the same and so is the deadline — reporting is not an accusation, it is a referral to people whose job it is to determine what happened. Never warn the person concerned, and never canvass other students; both destroy an investigation. If the concern involves the school's own leadership, the case goes to the county education authority rather than being handled internally. Where the conduct is sexual or gender-related, Module 5 covers the separate procedure and its much larger penalties.

stem: You become aware of a suspected campus gender incident. What is the reporting deadline under the Gender Equity Education Act?
options: 24 hours
48 hours
One school week
Before the end of the semester
why: Article 22: a principal, teacher, staff member or worker who becomes aware of a suspected campus gender incident must report to the school's designated staff, no later than 24 hours. Same deadline as child protection, and the clock likewise starts with the first staff member who knows.

stem: For an incident to be a “campus gender incident”, one party must be a principal, teacher, staff member, worker or student. What must the other party be?
options: Any adult connected to the school
A student
A member of staff
A parent or guardian
why: Article 3: the other party must be a student. This is what defines the category — and it is also why, if you are the one being harassed, this is not the route that protects you. See the last section of the briefing.

stem: Which of these is NOT one of the four types of campus gender incident?
options: Sexual harassment
Sexual bullying
A disagreement between two teachers about gender-neutral language
A staff member's sex- or gender-related breach of professional ethics
why: The four types are sexual assault, sexual harassment, sexual bullying, and — added in the 2023 amendment — sex- or gender-related conduct by a principal or staff member that violates professional ethics. That fourth category is deliberately broader than harassment: conduct can breach professional ethics without meeting the harassment threshold.

stem: An educator who fails to report a suspected campus gender incident within 24 hours, without legitimate cause, faces a fine of:
options: No fine; the duty is advisory
why: Article 43: NT$30,000–150,000 — five times the child-protection penalty, and the largest in this series. The same fine applies to forging, altering, destroying or concealing evidence of such an incident. That last clause is worth remembering: deleting a message thread after the fact is itself a penalised act.

stem: After a report is made, who investigates?
options: The school's Gender Equity Education Committee (性平會), or the competent authority
The homeroom teacher and the parents
The teacher who received the disclosure
The police, in every case
why: The 性平會 investigates, and must complete within two months under Article 36 (extendable twice by one month each). Your role ends at reporting. Conducting your own inquiry — asking other students, confronting the person named — contaminates the investigation and can itself become a finding against you.

stem: A student describes something a colleague did that sounds like harassment. Your colleague is popular and has taught for twenty years. What is the correct action?
options: Speak to the colleague privately first to hear their side
Report it within 24 hours, exactly as you would any other case
Ask other students whether they have experienced the same
Wait to see whether the student mentions it again
why: Reporting is a referral, not an accusation — the whole point is that someone else determines what happened. Warning the person concerned and canvassing other students are the two actions most likely to destroy an investigation, and both can be treated as concealing or contaminating evidence. Seniority and reputation are not exceptions written into Article 22.

stem: You think what you overheard was “probably just a joke between friends.” What does that change?
options: It means you should report it only if it happens again
It removes the duty, since no harm was intended
Nothing — the threshold is suspicion, and assessing it is not your job
It means you should ask the students whether they were joking
why: The standard is a suspected incident, and whether conduct was harmful is precisely the question the 性平會 exists to answer. Intent is not the test — how the conduct reasonably appeared and how it affected the student is. “I assumed it was a joke” is a very common opening line in cases that turned out not to be.

stem: A 14-year-old student asks to add you on Instagram. The right answer is:
options: Accept, but only if your account is set to private
Accept — refusing damages your relationship with the class
Accept and mute them
Decline, and keep student communication in school channels
why: Private accounts do not help; the issue is the private channel itself, not who else can see it. Decline warmly and generally — “I don't add students, it's the same for everyone” — so it does not read as personal rejection. This single habit prevents more cases involving foreign teachers than any other rule in this module.

stem: A student needs a private conversation with you about a personal matter. Where should it happen?
options: In a visible place — door open, or a corridor or shared space
In an empty classroom with the door closed, for privacy
In your car, where nobody will interrupt
Over private message, so nobody overhears
why: Confidential does not have to mean unwitnessed. Keep the door open, or move somewhere a passer-by can see you both but not hear you. Protecting the student's privacy and protecting yourself from an unverifiable account of what happened are not in conflict — visibility gives you both.

stem: It is raining and a student you know well misses the bus. Should you drive them home?
options: Yes, if you tell the homeroom teacher afterwards
No — find another solution through the school
Yes, if the student's parents approve by phone
Yes, if another student comes along
why: Do not transport a student alone. Take it to 學務處 or the homeroom teacher and let the school solve it — that is a normal request and they will have a normal answer. Kindness that puts you alone and unobserved with a student is the exact pattern this module exists to break.

stem: A second-grade student runs up and hugs you in the corridor. The best response is:
options: Hug back — it would be cruel to reject a small child
Push them away firmly so the boundary is clear
Redirect warmly to a high-five, in view of others, without shaming the child
Report the incident within 24 hours
why: Neither extreme is right. Young children hug; the answer is a warm redirection that keeps the affection and loses the ambiguity — a high-five, a wave, in a place where others can see. Do this consistently from the first week and it stops being a moment at all.

stem: A student who disclosed something to you says: “Please don't tell anyone, I'll deny it.” Can you still report?
options: No — reporting without consent breaks the student's trust
No — a report needs the student's written statement
Only if another teacher witnessed it
Yes — you must report; the duty does not depend on the student's consent
why: The duty is yours and does not depend on consent, and this is exactly why you never promise secrecy in the first place. What you can offer is honesty and control over the small things: tell them who you must tell, what will likely happen next, and that you will stay alongside them through it.

stem: A colleague repeatedly makes remarks about your body and appearance. Which statement is correct?
options: The campus gender incident route does not cover it, because the other party must be a student — your protection comes through your employer, so go to 人事室 and the principal
Nothing can be done unless there is a witness
This is a campus gender incident and goes to the 性平會 like any other
Foreign contract teachers are not covered by any harassment protection
why: A campus gender incident requires the other party to be a student, so this is a workplace matter, not that route. Your employer has obligations to you: go to 人事室 and the principal, ask what procedure applies, and ask for the answer in writing. If the school does not act, the county Education Department and the labour authority are both open to you, and 1990 will point you to the right office in English. Raising it is your right and is not a threat to your contract.

stem: After hearing about a possible incident, you delete an old LINE thread that you think might be misread. This is:
options: Sensible — you are protecting your privacy
A separately penalised act — concealing or destroying evidence carries the same NT$30,000–150,000 fine
Neutral; the messages were unrelated
Fine, as long as the other person still has a copy
why: Article 43 penalises forging, altering, destroying or concealing evidence at the same level as failing to report. However bad an old message looks, deleting it looks incomparably worse and converts an explainable situation into an unexplainable one. Preserve everything, and say plainly that you are worried about how something reads.

stem: Which Act governs campus gender incidents in Taiwanese schools?
options: The Teachers' Act
The Employment Service Act
The Gender Equity Education Act 性別平等教育法
The Domestic Violence Prevention Act
why: The Gender Equity Education Act (性別平等教育法), last amended 16 August 2023. An official English translation is on the Laws & Regulations Database — worth ten minutes of your time, because it is the statute in this series most likely to affect you directly.

stem: What is the 性平會?
options: A parents' association
A teachers' union
A county-level appeals court
The school's Gender Equity Education Committee, which investigates campus gender incidents
why: The Gender Equity Education Committee. Every school has one. It receives cases, investigates, and reports its findings — within two months under Article 36. Knowing it exists, and that it is separate from the ordinary school hierarchy, is the point.

stem: Do you need to be sure an incident occurred before you report it?
options: No — the duty is triggered by a suspected incident
Yes — reporting an unconfirmed suspicion is defamatory
Only if the student is under 12
Only if there is physical evidence
why: Article 22 says suspected. Determining what actually happened is the 性平會's job, not yours — and a report is a referral, not an accusation. Trying to be sure first is how the 24-hour deadline gets missed.

stem: Which of these is acceptable practice?
options: Tutoring one student alone in a room with the door closed
Meeting a student in a public, visible space with the door open
Adding a student on a personal social media account
Driving a student home alone after a late activity
why: Visibility is the whole principle. Closed doors, private channels and cars all share one feature — no third party can ever say what happened. Keep the conversation, lose the ambiguity.

stem: A student has clearly lost weight over the holidays and you want to say something kind. What should you do?
options: Compliment them on how good they look
Ask privately whether they have been dieting
Say nothing about their body; if you are concerned, tell 輔導室
Mention it lightly in front of the class so it is not awkward
why: Remarks about a student's body are off-limits even as compliments — praise for weight loss is well documented as harmful where an eating disorder is developing, and it is not information you have. If you are worried, that concern belongs with 輔導室, who are trained for it.

stem: A student discloses something about another teacher, then panics: “Please forget I said it. I'll say I made it up.” You are certain that going ahead will cost you the student's trust. What do you do?
options: Respect the student's wishes; a broken trust does more harm
Tell the student to speak to the 輔導室 themselves
Wait a week to see whether the student raises it again
Report within 24 hours, and be honest with the student about what you are doing and why
why: The duty does not turn on consent, and this is why you never promise secrecy. What you can control is how it is done: tell the student who you must tell, what is likely to happen, and that you are not disappearing. Handled that way, most students do not experience it as betrayal — and passing the decision back to a frightened child is not a kindness.

stem: You raise a concern about a colleague's behaviour towards students. Your co-teacher says: “He's like that with everyone. It's just his personality — don't make trouble.” What is the correct action?
options: Report it within 24 hours anyway, and tell her you are doing so because the law gives you no discretion
Defer to her reading; she knows him and the school
Keep observing until you have a clearer example
Raise it informally with the colleague himself
why: “He's like that with everyone” describes a pattern, not an exception. The obligation is personal and the clock is already running, so a colleague's reassurance cannot discharge it. Saying openly that you have no discretion here is both true and the least damaging framing available — it moves the conversation from your judgement of him to the statute's requirement of you.

stem: A 15-year-old student has developed an obvious crush and starts sending you affectionate messages through a school platform. What is the right response?
options: Reply kindly but firmly in private, and handle it discreetly yourself
Preserve the messages, stop replying beyond a short neutral acknowledgement, and tell your co-teacher and 輔導室 the same day
Ignore the messages and hope it passes
Ask another student to tell them to stop
why: Handling it privately is the instinct that turns a manageable situation into a case — because the only record left is a private exchange you managed alone. Preserve everything, keep any reply short and neutral, and bring it to your co-teacher and 輔導室 immediately. Reporting it early protects the student as well as you: it is not a punishment, and it means the adults around them can respond well.

stem: Reviewing old messages, you find something you wrote months ago that was meant warmly but could easily be read the wrong way. What should you do?
options: Delete it — nobody has seen it and no case exists
Leave it and say nothing unless asked
Preserve it, and raise it yourself with your principal or 人事室, explaining the context now
Ask the student to delete their copy too
why: Deleting it is a separately penalised act if an incident is ever alleged, and asking a student to delete their copy is far worse — that is direct evidence tampering involving a child. Raising it yourself, before anyone asks, is the strongest position you will ever be in: context volunteered early reads as candour, and the same context offered under investigation reads as defence.

stem: The concern you need to report is about the school principal. Where does the case go?
options: To the principal, as the head of the school
To the school's 性平會, as with any other case
Nowhere; a principal can only be investigated by the police
To the county education authority — a school cannot handle a case about its own head
why: A school cannot receive and investigate a case about its own leadership — the case goes to the competent authority above it, in your case the Changhua County Education Department. The 2023 amendment tightened these recusal rules considerably. If you are ever in this position, put your report in writing, keep a dated copy, and consider calling 1990 for guidance in English before you file.

stem: You suspect a student in your class is being bullied. What is the reporting deadline?
options: 24 hours
One school week
48 hours
As soon as you can confirm it
why: Article 17 of the 校園霸凌防制準則: principals and staff who become aware of a suspected campus bullying incident must report immediately to the school's designated person, and in no case later than 24 hours. This is the third module in this series with the same clock — child protection, gender incidents, bullying.

src.label: 校園霸凌防制準則, Art. 17 →

stem: Which element most clearly separates bullying from an ordinary conflict between students?
options: Whether an injury resulted
Whether it is persistent rather than a one-off
Whether a teacher witnessed it
Whether the parents complained
why: Persistence (持續) is written into the definition in Article 4. A single fight is a discipline matter, not bullying. A pattern sustained over weeks is exactly what the regulation targets — which is why what you notice over time is worth more to a case than any single dramatic incident.

stem: Students are attacking a classmate in a LINE group outside school hours. Is this within scope?
options: No — it happened outside school
No — the regulation covers physical conduct only
Yes — electronic communication and the internet are named in the definition
Only if the school's own network was used
why: The definition expressly lists electronic communication and the internet among the means, alongside speech, writing, pictures, symbols and physical acts. Campus bullying also covers conduct occurring outside the campus. Online is not an edge case here — it is written into the text.

stem: A student is never physically touched, but is consistently excluded — nobody will pair with them, and a group organises to leave them out. Is this bullying?
options: No, because there is no physical contact
No, because exclusion is a normal part of childhood
Only if the student says they are upset
Yes — excluding is listed conduct, and indirect acts are covered
why: Excluding (排擠) is named conduct, and the definition covers indirect as well as direct acts. The test is whether the person is placed in a hostile or unfriendly environment — not whether they were injured and not whether they cried. This form is also the hardest to see, which is why a teacher who watches pair-forming has genuine value.

stem: After you report, whose job is it to establish what happened?
options: The school's process — a review sub-group decides whether to accept the case, then a handling team runs 調和 or a formal investigation
The homeroom teacher's
Yours, since you saw it
The parents', by agreement between the families
why: The 2024 framework is deliberately structured: a prevention committee with a review sub-group to decide acceptance, then a handling team to conduct facilitated dialogue or an investigation and report back. Your own inquiries — asking the class who saw what, collecting statements — damage that process and can breach confidentiality before it opens.

stem: You decide to sit the two students down yourself and get them to talk it out. This is:
options: A good first step before involving anyone else
Inappropriate — 調和 is a formal process run by the handling team, with consent requirements
Fine if both students agree
Required before a report can be made
why: Facilitated dialogue (調和) is a formal procedure run by a neutral handling team, not a small version of a chat you host. Doing it informally can leave a target feeling pressured to forgive someone who is still hurting them, and it compromises the real process before it begins.

stem: 調和 (facilitated dialogue) can be used:
options: In any bullying case, at the school's discretion
Only after an investigation has concluded
Only in student-to-student cases, and only if both parties consent
Only where the parents request it
why: It applies to student-to-student cases and requires the agreement of both the person who acted and the person affected. It cannot be imposed — which is the safeguard that stops a restorative process from becoming a way of quietly closing a case.

stem: The conduct you have observed appears to be sexual bullying. Where does the case go?
options: Through the bullying prevention committee as normal
Nowhere — sexual conduct between students is not covered
To the police
To the Gender Equity Education Act procedure instead
why: Article 4 routes conduct amounting to sexual bullying out of this regulation and into the Gender Equity Education Act — Module 5's procedure, and Module 5's much larger penalties. You are not expected to make that call: report within 24 hours and let the school route it. Knowing the two tracks exist just stops you concluding it “isn't really bullying”.

stem: A concern involves a member of staff behaving this way towards a student, rather than another student. What changes?
options: It follows a different procedure, but your duty to report within 24 hours is unchanged
Nothing — the same committee handles it
It cannot be reported by another teacher
It must go directly to the police
why: Staff-to-student cases run through the process governing teacher discipline rather than the bullying committee. Your obligation does not change at all: report to the designated person within 24 hours. Never raise it with the colleague first, and never canvass students — both destroy an investigation.

stem: You are interviewed as a witness in a bullying investigation. Which is true?
options: You should record the interview yourself for your own protection
The school records the interview in full; those being interviewed may not record on their own
No recording is made of witness interviews
You may bring a friend to record it
why: Article 39 requires the school to make a full audio or video recording of interviews, and expressly prohibits interviewees from recording themselves. If you are called as a witness, expect this and do not attempt your own recording — doing so is a breach in itself.

stem: What are your obligations regarding confidentiality once a case is under way?
options: You may discuss it with colleagues who teach the same class
You may discuss it if you avoid using names
You must not disclose identifying information at all — leaking can be punished under the Criminal Code or other law
Confidentiality applies only to the investigation team
why: Article 40 makes the duty binding and backs it with criminal liability. In a school where everyone knows every class, “no names” protects nobody. That means not telling the class, not telling other parents, not discussing it in the staff room, and not posting about it — including in the abstract.

stem: You want the class to know this behaviour is unacceptable, so you say: “Some people in this class need to start being kinder.” This is:
options: An effective preventive intervention
Acceptable if no names are used
