Required as part of prevention education
Unhelpful — it signals to the target that you know and are not acting, and tells everyone else who it is about
why: Everyone in the room decodes it instantly, including the target — who learns that an adult knows and has responded with a vague remark. Anti-bullying messages belong in planned lessons and in the school's prevention programme. Responses to an actual incident belong in a report and in the things you change.

stem: While the school's process runs, what is genuinely within your control?
options: Seating, grouping, and assigning pairs rather than letting students choose
Nothing — you must not interfere in any way
Speaking to both sets of parents
Moving the target to a different class
why: You control your room. Assigning pairs rather than letting students self-select is not a minor adjustment: for a child who is never chosen, it is the difference between a lesson they dread and a lesson they can sit through. It also requires no permission, breaches no confidentiality, and can start in your next lesson.

stem: What kind of record is most useful to a bullying investigation?
options: Your assessment of which student is at fault
Dated, factual notes on what you observed over a period of weeks
Statements collected from other students
Photographs of the students involved
why: Persistence is the element the definition turns on, so a series of small dated entries evidences it far better than one dramatic account. Record what you saw and heard, not your conclusions about who is to blame — and do not gather statements from students, which is investigating.

stem: Campus bullying (校園霸凌) covers conduct occurring:
options: Inside the school grounds only
During school hours only
Both inside and outside the campus
Only where a teacher was present
why: The definition covers bullying by school staff or students against students, occurring inside or outside the campus. Combined with the express inclusion of the internet, that means a group chat at 10 p.m. on a Sunday is squarely within scope.

stem: Who should receive your report first?
options: The county Education Department
The police
The parents of the student affected
The school's designated person, who then reports to the competent authority
why: Article 17 sets the chain: staff report to the school's designated person, who reports upward to the competent authority — the whole chain within 24 hours. Find out who that person is at your school before you need them, exactly as in Module 4.

stem: Does the student have to be physically injured for it to be bullying?
options: No — the test is whether they are placed in a hostile or unfriendly environment
Yes — some harm must be demonstrable
Only for cases involving younger students
Yes, unless the conduct occurred online
why: The definition ends on the effect: placing the person in a hostile or unfriendly environment. Injury is not required, and neither is a visible reaction. Many targets work very hard at showing nothing at all.

stem: A student tells you that someone else — not them — is being bullied. What do you do?
options: Ask the student for more details first so your report is complete
Report it within 24 hours, exactly as if you had seen it
Suggest the student tell the homeroom teacher themselves
Wait to see whether you observe it yourself
why: The duty is triggered by becoming aware of a suspected incident, however you became aware. Do not interview the student for detail — that is investigating. Thank them, tell them you have to pass it on, and pass it on. A student who reports and sees nothing happen does not report again.

stem: The students involved say they were “only joking.” How does that affect the analysis?
options: It ends the matter — bullying requires intent to harm
It halves the seriousness of the case
It does not resolve it: teasing is listed conduct, and the test is the effect on the other person
It matters only if a teacher witnessed the exchange
why: The conduct must be deliberate, but teasing (戲弄) is expressly listed among the named behaviours, and the definition turns on whether the other person is left in a hostile or unfriendly environment. “We were only joking” is the most common thing said in these cases and settles nothing — which is precisely why the assessment is not left to you.

stem: Over six weeks you have watched one student consistently left out, spoken over and quietly mocked. There is no single incident you could point to. What should you do?
options: Keep observing until you have one clear incident to report
Mention it informally to the homeroom teacher and leave it there
Raise it with the students involved directly
Report the pattern now, with your dated notes — persistence is the element the definition turns on
why: Waiting for a single dramatic incident misunderstands the definition: the pattern is the case. Six weeks of dated observations evidence persistence in a way one incident never could, and they are exactly what a handling team cannot reconstruct on its own. This is also the situation in which a foreign teacher's view of a class is genuinely irreplaceable.

stem: The student being targeted begs you not to report it: “It'll get so much worse if you do.” What is the right response?
options: Report it, tell them honestly that you have to and what will happen next, and change what you control in your own lesson immediately
Respect their wish; they understand the situation better than you
Agree to wait two weeks and review
Ask them to tell 輔導室 themselves
why: The duty is not conditional on consent, and this fear is usually well founded — which is a reason to make the report carefully, not to skip it. Be honest about what you must do, tell them who will know, ask 輔導室 what support they will get, and change seating and grouping in your room the same week so that something visibly improves rather than only becoming more official.

stem: You raise it with your co-teacher, who says: “They're children. They'll sort it out among themselves.” What should you do?
options: Defer to her; she knows these students far better than you
Report it within 24 hours anyway, and tell her you are doing so because the regulation gives you no discretion
Keep observing and raise it again in a month
Take it straight to the principal
why: Her reading may even be right about these particular children — but Article 17 does not give either of you the discretion to make that call, and the clock is already running. Framing it as “the rule gives me no choice” rather than “I disagree with you” is both true and the version of this conversation that leaves the working relationship intact.

stem: A parent asks you what is happening in a bullying case involving their child's class. You know some of it. What do you say?
options: Share what you know, since the parent has a legitimate interest
Share it without using names
Say that you cannot discuss it and that the school is the right place to ask — then tell your principal about the approach the same day
Say you know nothing about any case
why: Confidentiality is legally binding and backed by criminal liability, and omitting names protects nobody in a school where everyone knows every class. Decline, redirect to the school, and tell your principal the same day — leadership should hear about a parent approach from you first, not later from the parent.

stem: You reported a case a month ago. Nothing visible has changed, and the target tells you it is still happening. What is the correct action?
options: Accept that the process has run and the school has decided
Advise the family to make a formal complaint
Confront the students responsible yourself
Report the new incidents — each fresh incident is its own report, on its own 24-hour clock
why: You are generally not told the outcome, so silence tells you nothing about what has happened. What continues to be yours is the new information: each fresh incident is a fresh report with its own deadline. Keep the dated log running, ask 輔導室 what support the target is receiving, and keep changing what you control in your own room.

stem: Parents signed the school's image consent form at the start of the year. You post a photo of your class on your personal Instagram. Is that covered?
options: No — the consent covers the school's stated purposes, not your personal account
Yes, as long as you do not name anyone
Yes — consent was given for photographs of the students
Yes, if the account is private
why: Personal data may be used within the necessary scope of the specific purpose families were told about. That purpose is the school's, not yours. “No names” and “private account” do not convert an outside-purpose use into an inside-purpose one — and you have not read the form, so you do not actually know what it says.

stem: Which of these is NOT personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act?
options: A student's photograph
A grammar worksheet you wrote yourself
A student's family circumstances
A student's grades
why: Names, photographs, grades, health information, counselling records and family circumstances are all personal data about an identifiable person. Your own worksheet is your work — a copyright question, not a privacy one.

stem: You want to photocopy two pages from a published textbook for your class. Under the Copyright Act this is:
options: Prohibited without the publisher's written licence
Permitted only for material more than ten years old
Generally permitted — Article 46 allows reproduction within a reasonable scope for school teaching
Permitted only if you credit the author on every page
why: Article 46 allows a school and its teaching staff to reproduce published works within a reasonable scope for the needs of school teaching. “Reasonable” is doing real work in that sentence — a couple of pages for your lesson, not a whole book, and not a substitute for buying the class set.

stem: You then upload the same two pages to your public teaching blog so other teachers can use them. This is:
options: Also covered by Article 46, since the purpose is still educational
Fine if you add a note saying it is for educational use
Fine because the blog earns no money
Not covered — public transmission is a separate right that classroom fair use does not reach
why: This is the single most useful distinction in the module: legal in your classroom does not mean legal on the internet. Uploading is 公開傳輸 (public transmission), a separate right, and the teaching exceptions are written around the needs of a class — not around distribution to the world. Non-commercial and well-intentioned do not change the analysis.

stem: A parent messages you directly asking how their child is doing. The best response is:
options: Reply briefly and politely, redirect substantive matters to the homeroom teacher, and tell your co-teacher that the contact happened
Do not reply at all
Give a full account — parents are entitled to know
Reply only if the homeroom teacher approves each message
why: Warmth costs nothing and silence reads as rudeness, but the 導師 is the school's channel to families and holds the full picture. Telling your co-teacher matters as much as the reply itself: they should never learn about a parent contact from the parent.

stem: At a parent meeting, one parent asks about a different child in the class who has been having problems. You should:
options: Answer generally without using the child's name
Decline to discuss another family's child at all
Answer only if the other child's parent is not present
Redirect the question to the homeroom teacher and then answer briefly
why: There is no version of this that is acceptable, including the careful-sounding ones. In a class of thirty, “a child who has been struggling recently” identifies someone to everyone in the room. Decline, kindly and without explanation.

stem: Which of these ways of returning test results is appropriate?
options: Reading scores aloud in class order
Posting a ranked list on the classroom wall
Handing papers back face-down, or individually
Asking students to swap and mark each other's, then announce
why: A student's grades are personal data, and a classroom is a public place. Face-down or individual return costs you nothing. Public ranking is also poor teaching quite apart from the privacy question — see Module 3 on punishment tied to academic results.

stem: A student produces a wonderful poster. You want to put a photo of it on your public blog. What matters?
options: Nothing — you set the task, so the work is yours
Only whether the student's name is visible
Only whether the school logo is visible
The work belongs to the student — ask before displaying it publicly, and consider the privacy question separately
why: Two separate issues, both real. Copyright in a student's own work belongs to the student, so displaying it publicly is a permission question. And if their name or handwriting or face appears, the privacy analysis runs in parallel. Asking the student — and the school — takes a minute.

stem: You are leaving Taiwan and want to keep your photographs of the students as a memento. The right thing to do is:
options: Delete them — they were collected for a purpose that ends with the job
Keep only the ones where faces are unclear
Keep them privately; you will never post them
Ask each student individually for permission to keep them
why: The images exist because of the role, and the role is ending. Keeping a private archive of identifiable children from a job you have left is difficult to justify to anyone who asks later, and impossible to justify to a family. Take photographs of the school gate, the staff room, your colleagues instead — those are yours.

stem: A parent asks you to tutor their child privately at weekends, offering good pay. This is:
options: Fine, since it is outside school hours
A permit question, not a scheduling question — teaching outside your permitted employment needs separate authorisation
Fine if the principal knows
Fine if you do not charge
why: Straight back to Module 1: your permission to work is tied to your employer, and your principal cannot widen it. Decline warmly and generally — “I'm not able to teach outside school, it's the same for everyone” — so it does not read as a judgement about that family.

stem: In a staff LINE group you write: “Xiao-Ming really struggled again today, I think something's going on at home.” This is:
options: Fine — it is an internal staff channel
Fine because you are raising a genuine concern
Poor practice — named speculation about a child's home life should go to the homeroom teacher or 輔導室, not a group chat
Fine as long as no parents are in the group
why: The concern is right and the channel is wrong. Group chats are forwarded, screenshotted, and read by people who joined later. Say it to the homeroom teacher or 輔導室 directly — and if you suspect actual harm, Module 4's 24-hour duty applies and a group chat is certainly not the route.

stem: You want to show a short YouTube clip in your lesson, then post your own recording of the lesson online. Which part is the problem?
options: Both are problems
Neither is a problem
Showing the clip in class
Posting the recording online, because it redistributes the clip
why: Playing material in class for teaching purposes is generally within scope. Posting a recording that contains it is redistribution — and if students are visible or audible, you have added a privacy question on top of the copyright one. The lesson is the permitted setting; the upload is a different act.

stem: At a dinner, someone you have just met asks which school you teach at and about the students there. The safest habit is:
options: Name the school but talk about students only in general terms
Answer fully; it is public information
Answer nothing at all and change the subject
Answer only if they are also a teacher
why: Your workplace is not a secret and refusing to say where you work is strange. What does not travel is anything about identifiable children — no stories about a particular student, however funny or moving, told to people who can work out which school and which class.

stem: You realise a post from six months ago includes a clearly identifiable student. What should you do?
options: Leave it; removing it now would draw attention
Take it down first, then tell your co-teacher or principal the same day
Delete it quietly and say nothing
Ask the student's parents directly whether they mind
why: Remove it, then report it — in that order, the same day. A post taken down by the person who posted it and disclosed voluntarily is an ordinary correction. The identical post found by a parent later is an incident, and by then you are explaining rather than telling. Do not contact the family yourself.

stem: Under the Personal Data Protection Act, schools may use student data:
options: For any educational purpose they consider reasonable
However they wish, once consent has been signed once
Within the necessary scope of the specific purpose that families were told about
Only with fresh written consent for every single use
why: Purpose and necessity are the two limits, and families must be told the purpose at the point of collection. Neither “it's educational” nor “they signed something in September” is a general licence.

stem: Who is the school's normal channel for communication with families?
options: The English teacher, for anything about English
The Personnel Office
The principal
The homeroom teacher 導師
why: The 導師 holds the relationship, the Chinese and the whole picture of that child. Going around them is not a shortcut — it produces two versions of the school's message and undercuts the person who has to live with the family all year.

stem: Which is the clearest statement of the copyright rule for teachers here?
options: Copying for your class is generally allowed; putting the same thing on a public website is not
Nothing may be copied without written permission
Anything used for education is free to use anywhere
Copyright does not apply to material used in schools
why: Article 46 permits reproduction within a reasonable scope for school teaching. Public transmission — uploading — is a separate right that classroom fair use does not reach. If you remember one sentence from this module, make it this one.

stem: Before posting any photo involving students anywhere outside the school, you should:
options: Check that faces are not clearly visible
Ask your co-teacher or 教務處 first, every time
Check that you have not used any names
Post it and remove it if anyone objects
why: Ask first. The school knows which families have circumstances you will never be told about — a custody dispute, a protection order — and asking is what makes it impossible for you to be the person who caused that harm.

stem: Where should a concern about a particular student's home situation go?
options: The staff LINE group
A note to the parents
The homeroom teacher or 輔導室, directly
Your own diary, until you are sure
why: Direct, named, to the person whose job it is. Group chats get forwarded and screenshotted. And if what you suspect is harm rather than difficulty, Module 4's 24-hour reporting duty applies.

stem: Your school's own Facebook page regularly posts class photos, so you assume the same photos are fine on your personal account. Is that reasoning sound?
options: Yes — the school has clearly established that these photos may be published
Yes, provided you post the identical photos and add nothing
Yes, as long as you tag the school
No — the school publishes under its own consent arrangements and its own responsibility; that does not extend to you
why: The school is the data controller and answers for its own decisions; you are not covered by them. There is also a practical asymmetry worth noticing: the school can take a post down and tell every family it did. You cannot control where an image goes once it leaves your account, and a foreign teacher's account is usually followed by people with no connection to that community at all.

stem: A parent contacts you repeatedly, is warm and complimentary, and gradually starts asking about other students and about staff. The right response is:
options: Draw the line explicitly, redirect everything to the homeroom teacher, and tell your co-teacher and principal that this pattern is developing
Answer only the questions about their own child and ignore the rest
Keep the relationship friendly; a supportive parent is an asset
Block the parent
why: Warmth is exactly how this becomes difficult to refuse — each question is only slightly beyond the last. Quietly ignoring the awkward ones leaves you managing it alone, which is the worst position. Say plainly that you cannot discuss other students or colleagues, move the channel, and make sure the school knows before something is quoted back to you.

stem: You are applying for a job abroad and want to include classroom photos in your portfolio to show your teaching. What is the right approach?
options: Include them; a portfolio is a professional, private document
Use anonymised descriptions of what you taught, and photograph materials or the room rather than identifiable children
Include them with faces blurred
Ask the students to sign a release themselves
why: A portfolio circulates to people with no connection to the school and no accountability to those families, and “private document” describes intent rather than reality. Describe the lesson, show the materials, photograph the empty classroom — that demonstrates your teaching perfectly well. Students cannot consent to this on their own behalf, and asking them puts a child in an impossible position.

stem: A colleague asks you to send them the class photo folder because they are making a farewell video. What should you do?
options: Send it; they are a colleague at the same school
Send only the photos you personally took
Check with 教務處 how such material should be shared and used, rather than deciding it between the two of you
Refuse; the photos are yours
why: A farewell video may well be a normal school activity, properly consented for — that is precisely why the school should be the one saying so. Two teachers agreeing privately is how material ends up somewhere nobody authorised. Ask, and you also find out what the consent form actually covers, which is worth knowing anyway.

stem: A parent tells you their child is being treated unfairly by another teacher and asks what you have observed. You have in fact noticed something. The right response is:
options: Tell them what you saw; the child's welfare comes first
Deny having seen anything
Suggest the parent make a formal complaint and offer to be a witness
Do not give an account to the parent; take what you observed to the school through the proper route the same day
why: Both instincts here are wrong. Feeding a parent an account of a colleague's conduct puts you inside a dispute with no procedure and no protection for anyone — while denying what you saw abandons the child. The observation is real and belongs to the school, today. If what you saw might amount to improper discipline or bullying by staff, Modules 3 and 6 tell you it is reportable in its own right.

stem: You propose a new activity to your co-teacher. She says: “We'll study it and see.” 我們再研究看看. What has she most likely told you?
options: No — expressed in a way that avoids putting you in the wrong
She is interested and will get back to you
She needs more information before deciding
She wants you to write a formal proposal
why: Direct refusal puts the other person in the wrong, so it is often avoided. “We'll study it and see”, “that might be a little difficult”, “maybe next semester”, a pause and a change of subject, and enthusiastic agreement followed by nothing — all of these are usually no. Learning to hear it saves you from pushing.

stem: You suspect the answer was no, but you genuinely need to know. What is the best way to ask?
options: Ask again in the next staff meeting so there is a clear record
Ask privately, and offer an easy exit: “Is this worth pursuing, or should I drop it? Either is fine.”
Ask a third colleague what she really meant
Proceed as if the answer was yes and see what happens
why: Pushing in public forces someone to refuse you explicitly, which is the thing the indirect answer was designed to avoid — you get your answer and pay for it. Asking privately with an easy exit lets them be direct without cost, and most people will be.

stem: In Taiwanese school culture, “face” (面子) is best understood as:
options: Personal vanity
Emotional fragility
A person's standing in front of others — which is what lets them do their job
A formal system of rank
why: Standing is functional, not decorative: it is what allows a teacher to manage a class and a director to run a department. Damaging it does not merely embarrass someone, it makes their work harder — which is why the cost of a public correction is so much larger than it looks.

stem: Your co-teacher gives students a piece of grammar information you know is wrong. What should you do?
options: Correct it immediately so students are not misled
Correct it gently, framing it as a regional difference
Ask the students what they think the answer is
Say nothing, and mention it privately afterwards
why: A public correction in front of thirty students costs her the standing she needs to manage them, and they will remember the correction more than the grammar. Mention it afterwards and it can be fixed next lesson at no cost. One wrong item for one day is a smaller problem than a co-teacher who cannot rely on you.

stem: You intend to raise a problem at Friday's staff meeting. What should you do first?
options: Tell the person concerned beforehand
Prepare your points carefully and present them clearly
Circulate a written summary in advance
Nothing — meetings are the correct place to raise problems
why: Being blindsided in front of colleagues is the injury, usually more than the substance. Telling them first also frequently solves it before the meeting — and decisions here are often reached beforehand anyway, in conversations between the people concerned. That is where the work happens.

stem: A staff meeting is conducted entirely in Chinese. The most considerate approach is:
options: Ask your co-teacher to translate as it goes
Ask for a two-minute summary afterwards
Ask for the meeting to be held in English
Skip such meetings, since you cannot follow them
why: Live translation means your colleague cannot participate in her own meeting; a summary afterwards costs her two minutes. Attending even without understanding is also worth more than it seems — presence is read as commitment, and you will catch more over a term than you expect.

stem: You are invited to a staff dinner at the end of a hard term, and you are exhausted. The best move is:
options: Decline politely; nobody will mind
Decline but send a gift
Go, even if only for part of it
Go only if your co-teacher goes
why: Attendance is most of it, and leaving early is entirely normal. Turning up for an hour is read as being part of the group; a polite decline is read — usually wrongly, but consistently — as not wanting to be. This is the cheapest investment available to you all year.

stem: A colleague invites you to their wedding. You have no idea what is expected. What should you do?
options: Bring a wrapped gift instead of money, to be safe
Attend but give nothing, since you are a foreign guest
Give a generous amount to be safe
Ask a colleague what amount is appropriate for the red envelope
why: Asking is completely normal and nobody will think less of you for it — guessing is how people get it wrong in both directions. Amounts vary by relationship and region, and a colleague can tell you in one sentence. Attending matters more than the amount.

stem: A parent gives you an expensive gift after their child's exam results improve. What should you do?
options: Decline politely and tell your school
Accept and share it with the office
Accept graciously; refusing would cause loss of face
Accept but give something of equal value in return
why: Public-school staff are subject to rules on receiving gifts, and the timing here — after results — is exactly the pattern those rules exist for. Decline warmly, and tell your school so that the record shows you did. A red envelope is always declined. Small shared items like fruit for the office are a different matter.

stem: A colleague asks your age, your salary, and whether you are married. This is usually:
options: An intrusion you should politely shut down
Ordinary friendliness and an attempt to place you socially
A test of whether you will fit in
Preparation for a formal report
why: In many countries these questions are off-limits; here they are usually the small talk of getting to know someone. You are not obliged to answer any of them, and a light deflection with a question back works perfectly — but reading them as rudeness will make you lonely for no reason.

stem: You have a genuine complaint about how your co-teacher runs the class. The best first step is:
options: Write a clear, polite email so there is a record
Message it on LINE so it can be discussed asynchronously
Speak in person, privately, opening with the shared goal
Raise it with the Director of Academic Affairs
why: A written grievance is permanent, forwardable, and reads far colder than you meant it — and it is now a document rather than a conversation. In person, privately, opening with what you both want (“I want this class to go better for both of us”) and asking a question rather than making an accusation, is the version that can still end well.

stem: Going over a colleague's head to their director is:
options: Normal escalation, expected when a problem persists
The fastest route to a solution
Always inappropriate, whatever the issue
Expensive and rarely recoverable — reserve it for genuine necessity
why: It is the most expensive move available to you and the relationship usually does not recover. Escalate in order, and slowly. The clear exception is anything covered by Modules 4, 5 or 6 — where the duty runs regardless of hierarchy, and where saying plainly that you have no discretion is both true and protective of the relationship.

stem: In the lead-and-support model, which pattern suggests something has gone wrong?
options: The foreign teacher always leading and never planning
The lead role alternating between the two teachers
The co-teacher circulating and managing behaviour some lessons
Both teachers occasionally splitting the class
why: Support roles should alternate. If you are permanently the entertainer at the front and never in the planning, you are a resource rather than a colleague — and it usually means the conversation about roles never happened, not that anyone decided it should be this way.

stem: What single conversation is most likely to improve a co-teaching relationship?
options: An honest discussion about the students' weaknesses
Agreeing who plans, who leads, who handles behaviour, and when you swap
A shared social activity outside school
A written agreement about responsibilities
why: Most pairs never explicitly agree any of it: they improvise for a year, each quietly frustrated, each assuming the other prefers it this way. The conversation takes ten minutes and is worth having once per unit rather than once per year — and it is the one that changes what next year looks like.

stem: “可能有點困難” — “that might be a little difficult” — usually means:
options: The task is hard but achievable
More resources are needed
No
A decision has been deferred
why: It is one of the standard indirect refusals, alongside “we'll study it and see” and “maybe next semester”. Taken literally it sounds like an obstacle to solve; heard correctly it is an answer already given.

stem: When should you tell a colleague that you plan to raise their issue in a meeting?
options: Immediately after the meeting
There is no need to tell them
Only if the issue is serious
Beforehand, always
why: Always, and without exception. Being surprised in front of colleagues is the injury. Telling them first also often means the meeting is no longer necessary.

stem: Which is the best gift to bring back from a trip home?
options: Something to share in the staff room
An individual gift for your favourite student
An expensive gift for the principal
Nothing; gifts are inappropriate
why: Something shared for the office is always well received and creates no awkwardness for anyone. Individual gifts to students are a Module 5 problem, and an expensive gift to the principal creates precisely the situation the gift rules are written about.

stem: You do not understand what was decided in a Chinese-language meeting. What should you do?
options: Ask a student to explain
Ask your co-teacher for a short summary afterwards
Assume nothing relevant to you was decided
Ask for the minutes to be translated into English
why: A two-minute summary from your co-teacher is a small favour and the fastest route to the part that affects you. Assuming nothing relevant was decided is how foreign teachers find out about a schedule change from a student.

stem: What most strongly predicts a foreign teacher having a good year at a Taiwanese school?
options: Chinese language ability
Teaching experience
Turning up to things that are not lessons
Having a detailed contract
why: Sports day, the dinner, the rehearsal, the leaving party for someone you barely know. Each is an hour; together they are the difference between being a colleague and being a visitor. Language helps, but attendance is what people actually notice.

stem: You and your co-teacher have worked together all year without ever agreeing roles. You lead every lesson; she manages behaviour and rarely plans with you. It is May. Is it worth raising now?
options: No — the year is nearly over, raise it in September
Yes — but put it in writing so next year's arrangement is clear
No — the pattern is established and she clearly prefers it
Yes — ask the roles question now, framed around next year rather than as a complaint about this one
why: May is arguably the best moment: there is no crisis to resolve, and next year's arrangements are being thought about anyway. Framing it forward — “for next year, could we try swapping the lead?” — makes it a plan rather than a verdict on the year you both just had. And “she prefers it” is usually a guess neither of you has ever checked.

stem: Your co-teacher has become noticeably cooler over several weeks. You cannot identify anything that happened. What is the most useful response?
options: Ask a low-stakes, forward-looking question in private — and consider whether you corrected or contradicted her in front of anyone recently
Ask directly what you did wrong
Wait for it to pass; asking would make it awkward
Raise it with the Director of Academic Affairs
why: Waiting rarely repairs anything and “what did I do wrong?” asks her to voice a criticism, which is exactly what the indirectness was avoiding. A private, low-stakes opening gives her a way in without cost. And the specific thing worth auditing is public correction — a moment that felt trivial to you can have been expensive for her, in front of students or colleagues.

stem: It is May and nobody has mentioned your renewal. You raised it once in March and got “we'll see how things go.” What now?
options: Take it as a negative signal and start applying elsewhere
Ask 人事室 directly about the timeline and paperwork, separately from asking your principal about the decision
Wait; the school will tell you when it knows
Ask your co-teacher what she has heard
why: Splitting the question is the move. The administrative timeline is a factual matter Personnel can answer plainly, and asking about it is not asking anyone to deliver news. It also frequently reveals the real state of things — a school that has begun the paperwork has effectively decided. “We'll see” about a decision is not the same signal as “we'll see” about a proposal.

stem: A newly arrived foreign teacher at your school is visibly heading for trouble — skipping staff events, correcting colleagues publicly, complaining by email. What is the most useful thing you can do?
options: Leave it; it is not your business and they may resent the advice
Mention your concerns to the principal so the school can address it
Explain the patterns privately and early, as things you got wrong yourself
Send them a link to this module
why: Almost every returning teacher made some of these mistakes in their own first year, and hearing it from someone who did is completely different from hearing it as a correction. Do it privately, early, and as autobiography rather than instruction. Going to the principal turns a fixable habit into a file.

stem: Something in this module conflicts with what your school actually expects of you. What should you do?
options: Follow this module; it reflects the county's guidance
Follow whichever is more convenient
Ask the Education Department to rule on it
Follow your school — these are observed norms, not rules — and tell us about the gap
why: This is the only module in the series with no statute behind it, and a school that does things differently is not doing them wrongly. Your school wins. But tell us — a mismatch between what we describe and what schools actually do means this page needs fixing, and the people living it are the only ones who can say so.
